t.1.3.1: The two who drink the truth in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest, supreme abode, are called shadow and light by the knowers of Brahman, and also by those who keep the five fires and those who have thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire.
t.1.3.2: May we be able to master the Nāciketa fire, which is the bridge for those who sacrifice, and also that imperishable supreme Brahman, the fearless farther shore for those who wish to cross over.
t.1.3.3: Know the self as the lord of the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself; know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins.
t.1.3.4: The senses, they say, are the horses, and the sense-objects are the roads they range over. The self joined with the senses and the mind, the wise declare, is the enjoyer.
t.1.3.5: But he who is without understanding, whose mind is always unrestrained, his senses are uncontrollable, like the vicious horses of a charioteer.
t.1.3.6: But he who is possessed of understanding, with his mind always disciplined, his senses are under control, like the good horses of a charioteer.
t.1.3.7: But he who is without understanding, unmindful and ever impure, does not attain that goal, and goes on into saṃsāra.
t.1.3.8: But he who is possessed of understanding, whose mind is restrained, and who is ever pure, reaches that state from which he is not born again.
t.1.3.9: But the man who has understanding for his charioteer and holds the mind as the reins reaches the end of the road; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
t.1.3.10: Higher than the senses are the objects, and higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect, and higher than the intellect is the great self.
t.1.3.11: Higher than the Great is the Unmanifest; higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. Higher than the Puruṣa there is nothing at all; that is the culmination, that is the highest goal.
t.1.3.12: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by those of subtle vision through a keen and subtle intellect.
t.1.3.13: The wise one should restrain speech and mind; that he should restrain in the knowing self. The knowing self he should restrain in the great self, and that he should restrain in the tranquil self.
t.1.3.15: That which is soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, likewise tasteless, eternal and odourless, without beginning, without end, beyond the Great, and unchanging: having discerned that, one is freed from the mouth of death.
t.1.3.14: Arise, awake! Having drawn near, learn from the excellent one. Like the sharpened edge of a razor, hard to cross, so is the path hard to travel, the wise declare.
t.1.3.16: Having told and having heard the ancient tale of Naciketas, spoken by Mṛtyu, the wise man is glorified in the world of Brahman.
t.1.3.17: He who, being pure, causes this supreme secret to be heard in an assembly of brahmins, or at the time of the śrāddha rite, that becomes fit for infinity. That becomes fit for infinity.
